passage:
Hrithik,
Second semester here. You asked what it's like, honestly, so here it is.
My roommate did a summer coding camp in Class 11. My lab partner's uncle got her an internship with one phone call. When Kartik failed a subject, his parents just paid for a repeat course, no drama. I sit in the library till closing because the hostel room is also where I make calls home and sort out Maa's pension papers online.
Some nights I'm angry. It feels like they started the race fifty metres ahead and nobody even sees the line.
But then I remember: I'm the first from our lane to be here, and I got in with borrowed books and the tuition-sir who taught us free on Sundays. Nobody handed me that.
So, both. Angry and proud. Tell Sir I'm still doing his sums.
Tejas

qa.a: The lab partner's uncle got her an internship with one phone call.

qa.a: Angry because classmates started "fifty metres ahead" with help no one sees, and proud because Tejas got in, first from the lane, with borrowed books and free Sunday tuition.

qa.q: What could Tejas do with the anger so it doesn't take over?
qa.a: Tejas could keep naming it honestly, as in this letter, while leaning on the pride and on people like the tuition-sir who backed Tejas.

qa.q: How might the tuition-sir feel hearing "I'm still doing his sums"?
qa.a: The tuition-sir would probably feel proud and moved, seeing those free Sundays carry a student this far.

grounding: A first-generation student sees peers' hidden advantages and feels both resentment at the uneven start and pride in how far they have come.

passage: Aadhya, you asked for the real version for the magazine, so here it is. I'm Yash, final-year commerce, from a government school in a town you've probably never heard of. In first year I thought everyone here was just smarter. Then I noticed things. Friends failing a paper and saying, "No stress, Papa will get me into his friend's firm anyway." People with uncles in accounting checking their assignments. Me? When my phone broke in exam week, I borrowed one for ten days, because a new one meant my sister's fees. Sometimes I sit in placement talks and feel this hot resentment, like the track was marked differently for us. But I also topped accounts last semester. From that town. On a borrowed phone. I'm allowed to be proud of that too, right? Print that part.

qa.a: For ten days, in exam week.

qa.q: What does Yash feel during placement talks?
qa.a: Yash feels a hot resentment, as if the track was marked differently for students without safety nets.

qa.a: Yash is choosing to have the pride told alongside the disadvantage, so the story isn't only about what was missing.

passage: I'm Parveen, and Imran's been in my study group since first year. Last week the others were planning a beach trip: flights, a villa, "just ask your parents". Imran said he had shifts at the call centre that weekend. He always has shifts. He did his whole presentation on a phone because his laptop died and a new one wasn't possible "this month". When our professor praised it in front of the class, Imran smiled, a proper wide smile I've rarely seen. But in the canteen, when Rhea complained her father had "only" given her ten thousand for the trip, Imran's jaw tightened and he went very quiet. I can't know exactly what he feels. I think it's something like pride and something like anger, taking turns.

qa.q: Why did Imran do his whole presentation on a phone?
qa.a: Because his laptop died and a new one wasn't possible that month.

qa.q: What might Imran's tightened jaw in the canteen suggest?
qa.a: It suggests anger or resentment at how easily others get money and trips, though Parveen can't be sure.

qa.q: What could Parveen and the group choose when planning the next outing?
qa.a: They could plan something that doesn't depend on parents' money and check Imran's shifts first, so he isn't always the one saying no.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when the professor praised his presentation?
qa.a: He probably felt proud, shown by the rare wide smile, since he managed it on a phone without the tools others had.

grounding: A classmate watches a student who works shifts see peers' safety nets, showing flashes of both resentment and pride.

passage:
Week one of engineering college. Eshaan learnt that his lab partner Raghav had done two years of entrance coaching, owned a new laptop, and had an uncle who ran a software firm. Eshaan had studied from secondhand books at a government school; he was the first in his family at college.
Mid-semester. Raghav failed a quiz and shrugged. "Dad'll get me a tutor." Eshaan had failed the same quiz. He spent the night in the library, doing every problem twice. Walking back to the hostel at two a.m., he felt it bitterly: they had started at different lines, and nobody even seemed to notice.
End of semester. The results went up. Eshaan had passed every subject, only a little behind Raghav. The old sting came, and then something warmer. He rang home from the hostel corridor. "Amma, I passed everything. All of it." She cried. He grinned at the peeling wall.

qa.q: Where did Eshaan spend the night after failing the quiz?
qa.a: In the library, doing every problem twice.

qa.q: What did Eshaan feel on the walk back at two a.m.?
qa.a: He felt bitter resentment that he and Raghav had started at different lines while nobody else seemed to notice.

qa.q: At the end of the semester, what did Eshaan choose to focus on, and why did it matter?
qa.a: He felt the sting of comparison but chose to ring his mother and share his pride in passing everything, measuring how far he had come rather than only the gap.

qa.q: How might Raghav see the same semester?
qa.a: To Raghav a failed quiz was just a reason to get a tutor, so he may not realise how much harder the same result was for Eshaan.

grounding: A first-generation student sees a peer's coaching, laptop and family safety net, feels the race began at different lines, and also feels proud of how far he has come.

passage: Shreya, you rang me angry that your hostel friends fly home every long weekend while you save for the bus. Let your Vasudha Mami tell you something. In 1994 I was eighteen, at medical college, a tailor's daughter. Half my batch had doctor parents: textbooks at home, uncles who would "have a word" with a professor, fathers who paid if anyone failed. I photocopied chapters page by page. In second year, when a girl got a hospital posting through her father's phone call, I cried in the bathroom, furious. It wasn't fair, and it still isn't. But that same year I stitched my own white coat on Appa's machine, and I topped anatomy. Both things sat in me together, the anger and the pride. Keep both, beta. Don't let either one eat the other.

qa.q: What did Vasudha stitch on Appa's machine?
qa.a: Vasudha's own white coat.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha cry in the bathroom in second year?
qa.a: Vasudha was furious and hurt that a classmate got a posting through a father's phone call, a safety net Vasudha never had.

qa.q: What advice does Vasudha give Shreya, and why might it help?
qa.a: To keep both the anger and the pride without letting either eat the other, so Shreya can name the unfairness and still value the distance covered.

qa.q: How might Shreya hear this story right after an angry phone call?
qa.a: Shreya may feel understood rather than scolded, because the story admits the unfairness is real while showing someone who still went far 🤍

grounding: An elder recalls being a tailor's child among well-connected classmates, resenting their safety nets and feeling proud of the distance covered.
